# Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems

###### Abstract.

Agentic machine learning engineering (MLE) is an emerging AI4SE
application, targeting complex machine learning tasks and taking a step
toward the recursive self-improvement of AI systems. Recent agentic MLE
systems highlight the importance of collecting and leveraging insights
from closely-related MLE tasks: some systems condition code generation
on expert domain knowledge, which is implicitly curated from peer MLE
tasks; some systems have a loop of solving an MLE task, gathering
validation feedback, and refining their prompts, skills, or memory to
benefit future tasks. However, collecting and injecting insights is ad
hoc, and existing evaluations do not control the sources of insights,
leaving data leakage a threat to validity.

To close these gaps, we systematically study how insights assembled from
closely-related MLE tasks affect an agentic MLE system, and how their
effect depends on the type of insights and the way they are injected. We
first collect a new benchmark, MLE-InsightBench, consisting of 160
Kaggle competitions clustered into 12 domains. MLE-InsightBench is
designed to keep target task information out of the insights: one
competition from each domain is held out as a target task, and only the
remaining 148 competitions, none of which can have been influenced by
the target tasks (e.g., as a later edition of the same series or by
reusing their solutions), serve as source competitions. We then design
and implement an insight assembly agent, MLE-InsightForge, that explores
the source competitions, their top human-written solutions, and
writeups, and assembles them into three types of insights: 12 domain
insights (summarizing domain-level best practices), 148 competition
insights (describing competition-level winning solutions), and 16
improvement insights (detailing generic debugging and improvement
strategies). The extracted insights can be injected into an agentic MLE
system as skills, which the agent reads selectively on demand, or as a
playbook placed upfront in its initial context. In our evaluation, the
extracted insights improve the normalized private-test score of an
agentic MLE system by 123.9% over the baseline without insights. Further
controlled experiments show that: the three types of insights are
complementary, the better injection mode (skill vs. playbook) varies
across tasks, with skills being more cost-effective overall, and the
improvements from insights generalize across backend LLMs.

## 1. Introduction

Machine learning engineering (MLE) is the end-to-end work of turning a
dataset and a modeling objective into an executable machine learning
(ML) solution, including data inspection, model selection, validation
design, debugging, and compute allocation. ML solutions are typically
written in Python, as Jupyter notebooks or scripts ([Pimentel et al.,
2019](#bib.bib42); [Grotov et al., 2022](#bib.bib43)), and the SE
community has studied them as software artifacts with distinct
engineering challenges, such as data management, code quality, and
reproducibility ([Amershi et al., 2019](#bib.bib41); [Pimentel et al.,
2019](#bib.bib42); [Mostafavi Ghahfarokhi et al., 2024](#bib.bib9); [Jin
et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)). This makes ML solutions a natural target of
LLM-based coding agents, but also a challenging one. Existing code
generation benchmarks, including those for data science code, check a
generated function, notebook cell, or patch against tests or reference
outputs ([Lai et al., 2023](#bib.bib44); [Yin et al., 2023](#bib.bib45);
[Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib46)). An ML solution, in contrast, has no
test oracle: its quality is a metric value on unseen data, which can
only be estimated by executing long-running training code and improved
by repeatedly revising the solution.

Agentic MLE is an emerging application of coding agents in which LLMs
perform this work by iteratively writing, executing, and refining
code ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib2); [Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib1);
[Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)). Agentic MLE systems target complex ML
tasks, such as Kaggle competitions, and are a step toward the recursive
self-improvement of AI systems, since a system that can engineer ML
solutions can, in principle, contribute to building better AI
systems ([Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)). Evolution has been rapid: on
MLE-bench ([Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)), the fraction of competitions
in which the best system earns a medal grew from 17% in late 2024 to
over 60% in early 2026.

Recent agentic MLE systems highlight the importance of collecting and
leveraging insights from closely-related MLE tasks. Some systems
generate code based on expert domain knowledge, which is implicitly
curated from peer MLE tasks, either by searching the web for
state-of-the-art models and winning solutions of similar tasks ([Nam et
al., 2025](#bib.bib22); [Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)) or by drawing
on knowledge bases synthesized from open-source repositories,
competition platforms, and competition discussions ([Du et al.,
2026](#bib.bib25); [Du et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Nadafian et al.,
2026](#bib.bib17)). Other systems have a loop of solving an MLE task,
gathering validation feedback, and refining their prompts, skills, or
memory to benefit future tasks ([Grosnit et al., 2024](#bib.bib29); [Zhu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib21); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib16)).

However, in these systems, the process of collecting and injecting
insights is ad hoc: each system fixes one design, without a controlled
comparison of the alternatives. Each system collects insights from
different sources (web search, curated knowledge bases, or its own past
runs), represents them differently, and injects them into the agent’s
context in its own way. The ablation studies in these work typically
remove the entire insight source, e.g., the knowledge base or the cache
of prior wisdom ([Du et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib21)), which shows that insights help as a whole but leaves
open which types of insights contribute and how they should be injected.

Moreover, existing evaluations of these systems do not control for the
sources of insights, which leaves data leakage as a threat to validity:
the sources are chosen by each system rather than fixed by the
benchmark, so whether they exclude the target tasks is left to each
system and rarely verifiable. For example, web search at solving
time ([Nam et al., 2025](#bib.bib22); [Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib23))
can retrieve the winning writeups of the very competition being
evaluated, and knowledge bases built from competition platforms may
contain its solutions; even when the benchmark competitions are excluded
by name ([Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib21); [Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27)), closely-related editions of the same competition
series can remain. Such concerns were raised on the MLE-bench
leaderboard ([timeleft–, 2026](#bib.bib24)), which has since paused new
submissions to ensure fair and comparable results.

Figure 1. Overview of our study.Three side-by-side panels. The benchmark
panel lists Kaggle competition collection, domain clustering, the

To bridge these gaps, we systematically study how insights assembled
from closely-related MLE tasks affect agentic MLE systems, and how their
effect depends on the type of insights and the way they are injected.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")
illustrates the workflow of our study. We first build MLE-InsightBench
from Kaggle competitions with human-written solutions, i.e., gold-medal
teams’ notebooks and writeups, and group them into domains of
closely-related competitions. One competition of each domain is held out
as a target task, and only the remaining 148 competitions, all causal
non-descendants of the target tasks (i.e., none can have been influenced
by a target task, as a later edition of the same series or a competition
reusing its solutions could), serve as source competitions, which
mirrors practice and rules out insights derived from a target task’s own
winning solutions.

MLE-InsightForge then reads the descriptions, datasets, solution
notebooks, and writeups of the source competitions and assembles three
types of insights: competition insights on the decisions behind each
competition’s winning solutions, domain insights that reconcile them
into domain-level best practices, and improvement insights that connect
problems encountered during development to their resolutions. Each
insight consists of trigger–action items that a system can skip when
they do not apply, and is backed by records of its source passages. The
insights can be injected as skills, whose full text is read on
demand ([Anthropic, 2025](#bib.bib19)), or as a playbook in the initial
context ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18)).

On the 12 target tasks, the assembled insights improve the normalized
score of an agentic MLE system by 123.9% over the baseline without
insights, improving every task (significantly on 11) when injected as
skills; on an energy forecasting task, every run with insights beats the
best run without them, although none of its peer competitions involves
energy. Further controlled ablation studies show that the three types of
insights are complementary: each type alone significantly improves fewer
tasks (9, 8, and 8) than their combination (11). The improvements from
insights generalize across backend LLMs, including a stronger
proprietary LLM (GPT-6.1-Sol). However, the better injection mode varies
across tasks, with skills being more cost-effective overall, because
they reach a similar score with fewer input tokens (7.7% versus 25.2%
more than the baseline).

The main contributions of this work are threefold:

- •
  Benchmark. We collect MLE-InsightBench, a benchmark of 160 Kaggle
  competitions clustered into 12 domains, that provides a controlled
  environment for studying insights: its held-out split makes the
  sources of insights explicit and keeps target task information out of
  them.
- •
  Technique. We design and implement MLE-InsightForge, an agent that
  assembles evidence-based domain insights, competition insights, and
  improvement insights from human-written solutions and writeups, and
  injects them into agentic MLE systems as skills or playbooks.
- •
  Experiments. We systematically evaluate the impact of assembled
  insights on an agentic MLE system, including their overall
  effectiveness, the contributions of the three types of insights, the
  effectiveness and cost of the two injection modes, and the
  generalizability across backend LLMs.

## 2. Background

### 2.1. Agentic MLE Systems

validation, which trains a logistic regression with each rule held out
in turn and reports the mean AUC; training on all data; and test, which
predicts the test data and writes submission.csv.

An MLE task asks for an executable ML solution rather than only a fitted
model: it involves understanding the data and the metric, designing a
validation protocol, implementing preprocessing and training, diagnosing
failures, and producing an artifact that satisfies a submission
contract. These decisions are coupled: for example, the validation split
must reflect the deployment distribution, while model and feature
choices must respect runtime and memory limits. Competitions on
Kaggle ([Kaggle, 2026a](#bib.bib11)) expose MLE tasks through a common
interface consisting of a task description, datasets, an evaluation
metric, a compute environment, and a submission format.
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.1. Agentic MLE Systems ‣ 2. Background ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")
shows an example Kaggle competition, Jigsaw – Agile Community Rules
Classification ([Sorensen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib38)), which asks
whether a Reddit comment violates a given rule, including rules unseen
in training, together with a solution developed by an agentic MLE
system. The solution prepares features from the training data, validates
the model by holding out one rule at a time to mimic the unseen rules,
retrains on all training data, and writes the predictions for the test
data in the submission format.

MLE-bench ([Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)) turns 75 Kaggle competitions
into an offline benchmark: each competition’s training data is split
into new training and private-test sets, and a submission is graded
against the private-test labels and compared with the human leaderboard.
MLRC-Bench ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)) instead targets research
competitions held at ML conferences (e.g., NeurIPS and KDD Cup), but
contains only seven tasks. Neither benchmark specifies a temporal or
causal ordering among the tasks, i.e., there is no standard of which
other tasks may serve as sources of insights for a given task.

An agentic MLE system combines an LLM with tools for inspecting data,
editing code, executing experiments, and observing validation feedback,
typically following the ReAct pattern of interleaved reasoning and tool
use ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib7)). Beyond a single linear trajectory,
most recent systems search over candidate solutions. AIDE ([Jiang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib8)) maintains a tree of solutions that are drafted,
debugged, and improved; ML-Master ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib20))
explores such trees with Monte Carlo tree search, and AIRA-dojo ([Toledo
et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)) compares search policies and operators over
them; and FM Agent and LoongFlow ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib14); [Wan et
al., 2025](#bib.bib15)) evolve populations of solutions. Within a task,
these systems accumulate the code, scores, and reflections produced by
earlier candidates to guide later ones.

### 2.2. Insights in Agentic MLE Systems

We use _insight_ to denote a reusable, natural-language statement about
how to solve MLE tasks, derived from tasks other than the one being
solved. Recent systems obtain insights in two ways:

- •
  External knowledge: Insights are curated from external sources, such
  as solutions of similar MLE tasks on open-source repositories and
  competition platforms, API documentations, and forum discussions. Some
  techniques retrieve them on the fly, typically via web search (e.g.,
  MLE-STAR ([Nam et al., 2025](#bib.bib22)) and MARS ([Chen et al.,
  2026](#bib.bib23))); others build a knowledge base offline which is
  used for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) at solving time (e.g.,
  DS-Agent ([Guo et al., 2024](#bib.bib4)), MLEvolve ([Du et al.,
  2026](#bib.bib25)), AutoMLGen ([Du et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)),
  KAPSO ([Nadafian et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)), AIBuildAI-2 ([Zhang et
  al., 2026b](#bib.bib16)), and FM Agent ([Li et al.,
  2025](#bib.bib14))).
- •
  Self-improvement across tasks: Insights are distilled from the
  system’s own runs on previous tasks, usually generated by the agent
  itself or a separate surrogate agent. Examples include the accumulated
  memory of Agent K ([Grosnit et al., 2024](#bib.bib29)), the “prior
  wisdom” cache of ML-Master 2.0 ([Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib21)), and
  the takeaways of completed runs of AIBuildAI-2 ([Zhang et al.,
  2026b](#bib.bib16)) (which augments its external knowledge base).

Regardless of their source, insights reach the agent as text in its
context, and systems differ in when this happens. In the _skill_
mode ([Anthropic, 2025](#bib.bib19)), only compact metadata of each
insight (a name and a description) is placed in the context, and the
agent loads the full text on demand, a design known as progressive
disclosure. In the _playbook_ mode ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18)),
the insights are placed directly in the initial context as a playbook;
unlike a human-written prompt, a playbook is generated and maintained by
LLM agents. Skills save context but depend on the agent retrieving the
right insight, whereas playbooks make every insight available but
consume context even for irrelevant insights.

### 2.3. Data Leakage in Evaluating Agentic MLE Systems

An evaluation of an agentic MLE system suffers from data leakage when
the system has access, during solving, to information about the target
task that would not be available when solving a genuinely new task, most
notably the task’s own winning solutions. This differs from train–test
leakage in a generated solution, which some systems check ([Nam et al.,
2025](#bib.bib22); [Du et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)), and from
contamination of the backend LLM’s pre-training data, which several
papers acknowledge as a limitation ([Nam et al., 2025](#bib.bib22);
[Toledo et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)).

Insights are a direct channel for such leakage, because their sources
are usually the same public competition materials from which target
tasks are drawn. Web search at solving time is not reported to be
restricted to materials of other tasks ([Nam et al., 2025](#bib.bib22);
[Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)), and knowledge bases built from
competition platforms typically do not report whether the target tasks
were excluded ([Du et al., 2026](#bib.bib25); [Du et al.,
2025](#bib.bib26)). Some work did exclude the target tasks by
competition name ([Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib21); [Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27)), which does not cover later editions of the same
competition series. For example, MLE-InsightBench contains two AI
Mathematical Olympiad: Progress Prize 1 ([XTX Investments,
2024](#bib.bib36)) and Progress Prize 2 ([Frieder et al.,
2024](#bib.bib37)); if the first were a target task, excluding it by
name would still admit the second, whose description states that it
builds upon the first and one of whose gold-medal notebooks reuses code
from the winning solution of the first.

Cross-task memory raises a related concern about the order of tasks.
Accumulating experience over a sequence of tasks, i.e., online learning,
is not leakage by itself, as it mirrors how practitioners gain
experience over time. However, when the memory keeps accumulating across
the target tasks themselves, a task may be solved after another task
that it influenced. Avoiding leakage thus requires a chronological or
causal ordering of the tasks. These practices have been raised as a
fairness concern on the MLE-bench leaderboard ([timeleft–,
2026](#bib.bib24)), which is one of the reasons that the leaderboard has
paused new submissions. Contamination-free benchmarks in code generation
address a similar problem by evaluating only on problems released after
the model’s training cutoff ([Jain et al., 2025](#bib.bib39));
MLE-InsightBench
(§[3](#S3 "3. MLE-InsightBench: A Controlled-Environment Benchmark ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems"))
applies a similar principle to insight sources by using only
competitions that cannot have been influenced by the target tasks.

## 3. MLE-InsightBench: A Controlled-Environment Benchmark

In MLE-InsightBench, the source competitions are fixed and disjoint from
the target tasks: competitions are grouped into domains so that every
target task has closely-related peer tasks, and the split is fixed
before any insight is assembled.

A scatter plot of UMAP embeddings of the competition descriptions,
clustered into twelve clusters plus noise.

Figure 3. UMAP embeddings of the competition descriptions (12
clusters).A scatter plot of UMAP embeddings of the competition
descriptions, clustered into twelve clusters plus noise.

Competition collection. We collect Kaggle competitions using Meta
Kaggle ([Kaggle, 2026c](#bib.bib12)) and Meta Kaggle Code ([Kaggle,
2026b](#bib.bib13)). We retain competitions that are launched in 2020 or
later, use Python, have downloadable datasets, and have high-performing
self-contained solutions, and exclude playground competitions; a
solution counts as high-performing and self-contained if it received a
gold medal and uses no datasets other than the competition’s own. This
step yields 191 competitions, from which we manually remove 18 that do
not involve training ML models (simulation competitions and optimization
puzzles, such as the Santa series ([Reade and Oldacre,
2025](#bib.bib48))), leaving 173 candidate competitions. For each
competition, we collect the task description, the public writeups of the
teams ranked within the gold-medal zone of the leaderboard, and the
high-performing self-contained solution notebooks; we refer to the
latter two as the competition’s human-written solutions.

| Bioinformatics                       | CAFA 5 Protein Function ([Friedberg et al., 2023](#bib.bib69))   | F$`{}_{\text{max}}`$$`\uparrow`$ | Simple |
| Geography Retrieval and Localization | Image Matching 2025 ([Bellavia et al., 2025](#bib.bib57))        | mAA$`\uparrow`$                  | Simple |
| Medical Image Recognition            | RSNA Aneurysm Detection ([Rudie et al., 2025](#bib.bib70))       | AUC$`\uparrow`$                  | Code   |
| NLP                                  | Jigsaw Community Rules ([Sorensen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib72))    | AUC$`\uparrow`$                  | Simple |
| Physiological Signal Processing      | PhysioNet ECG Digitization ([Reyna et al., 2025](#bib.bib71))    | SNR$`\uparrow`$                  | Simple |
| Quantitative Finance                 | Mitsui Commodity Prediction ([Demkin et al., 2025](#bib.bib73))  | Sharpe$`\uparrow`$               | Code   |
| Scientific Signal Processing         | Ariel Data Challenge 2025 ([Yip et al., 2025](#bib.bib74))       | GLL$`\uparrow`$                  | Simple |
| Sport Tournament Prediction          | March Mania 2025 ([Sonas et al., 2025](#bib.bib75))              | Brier$`\downarrow`$              | Simple |
| Time Series Prediction               | Energy Behavior of Prosumers ([Eljand et al., 2023](#bib.bib35)) | MAE$`\downarrow`$                | Code   |

Table 1. Target tasks of MLE-InsightBench.

Domain clustering. We group the candidate competitions by clustering
their natural-language descriptions (overview and dataset description),
and then manually assign a human-readable label to each cluster. We
embed each description with harrier-oss-v1-27b ([Microsoft,
2026](#bib.bib31)), a text embedding model, by instructing it to cluster
competitions by ML task formulation and application domain. We then
reduce the embeddings to 11 dimensions with UMAP ([McInnes et al.,
2018](#bib.bib32)) (cosine distance, 20 neighbors) and cluster them with
HDBSCAN ([Campello et al., 2013](#bib.bib33)) (minimum cluster size 5,
minimum samples 3), which determines the number of clusters from the
data and leaves outliers unassigned. This yields 12 clusters and 7
outliers (unable to be clustered), as shown in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3. MLE-InsightBench: A Controlled-Environment Benchmark ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems").
We label each cluster by inspecting its member competitions and its most
distinctive terms under class-based TF-IDF ([Grootendorst,
2022](#bib.bib34)), and manually move the outlier WiDS Datathon
2022 ([Matthys et al., 2022](#bib.bib49)) into the cluster that contains
its other editions. Domains serve two purposes: they define the scope of
domain insights, and they ensure that every target task has
closely-related peer tasks from which insights can be assembled. We
exclude the Audio Recognition cluster, where none of its 8 competitions
satisfies the eligibility rule for target tasks described below, as well
as 4 other competitions without any writeup from the gold-medal zone,
and Jane Street Market Prediction ([cnyberg et al., 2020](#bib.bib47)),
whose dataset was available at our initial collection but is no longer
publicly accessible. The resulting MLE-InsightBench consists of 160
competitions in 12 domains, including a residual domain labeled _Other_
for the remaining outliers.

Held-out split. From each domain, we hold out one eligible competition
as a target task and use the remaining 148 competitions as source
competitions. A competition is eligible if the mean runtime of its
collected solutions is at most the 75th percentile of the runtimes of
all collected solution notebooks (25.5 minutes), which keeps the
evaluation within a fixed compute budget. We also manually mark some
competitions as ineligible where the executable environment for the
tasks are hard to replicate (e.g., using a huge dataset): AMP
Parkinson’s Disease Progression Prediction ([Kirsch et al.,
2023](#bib.bib50)), Drawing with LLMs ([Holbrook et al.,
2025](#bib.bib51)), Bengali.AI Speech Recognition ([Howard et al.,
2023](#bib.bib52)), Cornell Birdcall Identification ([Howard et al.,
2020](#bib.bib53)), and the BirdCLEF series (e.g., BirdCLEF+
2025 ([Klinck et al., 2025](#bib.bib54))). Among the eligible
competitions of the most recent year in a domain, we select the one with
the shortest solution runtime.

The resulting non-descendant split ensures that every source competition
is a causal non-descendant of its target task, i.e., a competition that
cannot have been influenced by the target task as a later edition of the
same series or reusing its solutions. This mirrors how insights would be
used in practice: an agentic MLE system facing a new task can draw on
prior experience, but not on experience derived from the new task
itself. While a chronological split (i.e., choosing the latest
competition of each domain) is more straightforward, it would reduce the
size of benchmark because the latest competitions sometimes are not
eligible as a target task, causing dropping of valuable source
competitions that could otherwise be used with our more careful split.
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3. MLE-InsightBench: A Controlled-Environment Benchmark ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")
lists the 12 target tasks, of which 9 are standard competitions with a
submission file and 3 are code competitions whose predictions are
produced through a competition-specific evaluation API.

Leakage control. MLE-InsightBench controls the sources of insights at
three points. First, the materials of the target tasks (datasets,
descriptions, writeups, and solutions) are excluded from insight
assembly, so no assembled insight can be derived from a target task’s
own winning solutions. Second, because the split only requires the
source competitions to be causal non-descendants of the target task,
earlier editions of a recurring competition series (e.g., March Machine
Learning Mania) remain legitimate source competitions, as they would be
for a practitioner. Third, the agentic MLE system under evaluation is
not given web-search tools and receives only the public data of the
target task; the private-test inputs are substituted only when the final
solution is graded (same as how Kaggle grades submissions), and the
private-test labels are never exposed.

## 4. Methodology

### 4.1. MLE-InsightForge: Insight Assembly Agent

MLE-InsightForge explores the descriptions, datasets, top human-written
solutions, and writeups of the source competitions and assembles three
types of insights from them. Separating _what_ insights are assembled
from _how_ they are injected
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2. Usage of Insights ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems"))
lets us vary the two independently.

#### 4.1.1. Agent Architecture

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4. Architecture of MLE-InsightForge: (a) the assembly agent and
(b) the four assembly stages.Two panels. Panel (a) shows an assembly
task, consisting of instructions and required sources, entering a ReAct
loop in which an LLM calls tools (reading files and notebooks,
inspecting datasets, running analyses in a sandbox, reading web pages,
PDFs, and repositories, and inspecting images and videos) and receives
observations; the tools access a read-only workspace with the
\SourceCompetitionsand the blacklist-filtered web; the LLM's context is
summarized when needed; the LLM submits a report to a validation step
that checks that all required sources were read in full and that each
insight has an evidence record, returning rejections to the LLM and
otherwise producing the insight text and evidence records. Panel (b)
shows four stages: competition insight assembly from each
\SourceCompetition, domain insight synthesis from the competition
insights and descriptions of a domain, improvement insight assembly from
writeups reporting a problem and its resolution, and clustering and
synthesis of the raw improvement insights into improvement insights.

MLE-InsightForge
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.1. Agent Architecture ‣ 4.1. MLE-InsightForge: Insight Assembly Agent ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")(a))
is a ReAct-style agent ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib7)), using
gpt-5.6-sol-pro as its backend LLM during our study. Each run of the
agent performs one assembly task, specified by the instructions of its
stage and the list of source files it must read. The agent’s tools read
files and notebooks, inspect datasets, run targeted analyses in a
sandboxed container (e.g., checking a preprocessing step or a validation
split claimed in a writeup, without rerunning the solution end-to-end),
and read the materials linked from writeups, such as web pages, PDFs,
code repositories, images, and videos.

Leakage prevention. The source materials are mounted read-only in the
agent’s workspace, which contains only the source competitions and not
the target tasks. Because some URLs in the source materials may also
link to the target tasks, web access goes through a blacklist of 1,985
URL patterns, which we extract from the descriptions, writeups, and
solution notebooks of the target tasks; links to Kaggle or GitHub the
competition’s or repository’s all sub-pages, while general documentation
and tutorial sites (e.g., library documentation and Wikipedia) are
manually exempted.

Evidence-based submission. The agent submits each insight through a
validated submission interface, which rejects the submission until the
agent has read every required source in full, otherwise returns the
incomplete insight to the agent for repair. To minimize hallucination,
the interface also requires an evidence record for every insight,
listing the original source passages it is based on; this ensures that
every insight can be traced back to its original source.

Assembly stages.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.1. Agent Architecture ‣ 4.1. MLE-InsightForge: Insight Assembly Agent ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")(b)
shows the four stages in which MLE-InsightForge runs. It first assembles
one competition insight per source competition and then synthesizes one
domain insight per domain from the competition insights of that domain.
Independently of these two types, it assembles raw improvement insights
from the writeups and consolidates them by clustering.

#### 4.1.2. Insight Types

MLE-InsightForge assembles 148 competition insights, 12 domain insights,
and 16 improvement insights, at a total API cost of \$903 USD at the
list prices of gpt-5.6-sol-pro (\$565, \$22, and \$317 USD for the three
types, respectively).

Competition insights. MLE-InsightForge first reads the description to
identify the objective, data, metric, and constraints, and then reads
every collected writeup in full. It consults the solution notebooks to
disambiguate implementation details and to check that a technique
claimed in a writeup is actually present, and inspects the datasets to
understand their characteristics and to check claims about them. The
resulting insight is organized around the decisions that distinguished
the winning solutions and states the conditions under which each
decision was made, rather than reproducing a particular solution, since
the insight is used for other tasks, to which a complete solution
tailored to the source competition’s data and metric does not transfer.

Domain insights. A target task has no insight of its own, but it shares
task properties with the other competitions in its domain.
MLE-InsightForge reads the descriptions and competition insights of all
source competitions in the domain and reconciles recommendations that
recur, complement each other, or conflict. It replaces
competition-specific prescriptions with conditional guidance; for
example, it associates a validation strategy with grouped subjects or
temporal deployment rather than as universally applicable. A domain
insight drops recommendations specific to a single competition, keeping
only those supported by several competitions or a task archetype.

A scatter plot of UMAP embeddings of the raw improvement insights,
clustered into groups plus noise.

Figure 5. UMAP embeddings of the raw improvement insights (15
clusters).A scatter plot of UMAP embeddings of the raw improvement
insights, clustered into groups plus noise.

Improvement insights. While the other two types describe the decisions
behind the final solutions, improvement insights capture how their
authors diagnosed and fixed problems along the way, by connecting an
observed problem (e.g., a validation split that does not match the
deployment setting, or an inference pipeline that exceeds the runtime
budget) to the resolution that fixed it. MLE-InsightForge first filters
writeups, with an LLM, for those that report both a concrete problem and
an actionable resolution. For each retained writeup, it then assembles
standalone insights, keeping only those whose outcome is directly
reported in the writeup; this step yields 1,068 raw improvement
insights. Because many improvement strategies recur across competitions,
exposing all of them individually would make them costly to discover and
highly redundant. We therefore cluster the raw improvement insights by
their descriptions, using the same approach as Domain Clustering
(§[3](#S3 "3. MLE-InsightBench: A Controlled-Environment Benchmark ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")),
and let MLE-InsightForge synthesize each cluster into one consolidated
insight under the same evidence constraints. Specifically, we embed the
text of each raw insight with harrier-oss-v1-27b, using an instruction
to identify the prediction task type, data modality, and application
domain that the insight targets, and cluster the embeddings with UMAP
(15 dimensions, 20 neighbors) and HDBSCAN (minimum cluster size 20,
minimum samples 5); we select these hyperparameters by a grid search for
clusters that are stable across random seeds, align with the data
modality and solution stage of the insights, and cover most insights.
This yields 15 clusters, and the outliers (4.9% of the raw insights)
form the residual cluster, as shown in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1.2. Insight Types ‣ 4.1. MLE-InsightForge: Insight Assembly Agent ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems").
MLE-InsightForge then synthesizes each cluster into one consolidated
improvement insight, including one for the residual cluster, resulting
in 16 improvement insights. A manifest records the member insights and
evidence of each cluster, so that every improvement insight remains
traceable to its raw ones.

#### 4.1.3. Insight Representation

A competition insight or domain insight consists of insight items
following the trigger–action pattern: a trigger (a task or data
condition that can be checked before acting), one recommended action,
and a rationale for its expected effect. Triggers are phrased in terms
of general task and data properties, so the agentic MLE system can skip
the items that do not apply to its task; conflicting findings are kept
as items with mutually exclusive triggers. The items are grouped by five
aspects of an ML solution (data modality, data, model, training, and
other) and ordered within each aspect by the cost of following them. An
improvement insight is a single item whose trigger is the observed
problem and whose action is the resolution, elaborated with its
limitations, cost, and how to check whether it worked. Each insight has
a name and a description; its evidence records are stored separately and
enter the context only if explicitly read.

### 4.2. Usage of Insights

#### 4.2.1. Base Agentic MLE System

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 6. Workflow of the agentic MLE system, with the insights
highlighted.A sequence diagram with five lifelines: orchestrator, MLE
agent, solution tree, submission validator, and insight skills. The
orchestrator starts the agent with the task, public data, the domain
insight, and the skills or playbook. In a loop, the agent calls the LLM,
executes solutions that become nodes of the solution tree, validates
submissions, and reads skills in skill mode. After the agent submits a
final node, the orchestrator replaces the public-test inputs with the
private-test ones, reruns the selected solution, and grades the
submission with the private-test labels.

The assembled insights can be injected into any agentic MLE system that
accepts textual context. In our study, we inject them into a ReAct-style
agentic MLE system that develops solutions in an isolated container with
access to the public data of the target task, whose workflow is shown in
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.2.1. Base Agentic MLE System ‣ 4.2. Usage of Insights ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems").
The system can inspect data, edit files, execute candidate solutions,
and validate submissions. Each execution is recorded as a node in a
solution tree, so the system can branch from an earlier candidate when a
modification fails, similar to AIDE ([Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)).
At the deadline, the selected solution is rerun from scratch on the
private-test inputs and graded outside the agent loop. Without insights,
this system is the Baseline of our evaluation
(§[5](#S5 "5. Evaluation ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")).

#### 4.2.2. Insight Injection Modes

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 7. Scope of the insights injected for a target task.A large
circle represents the current domain and contains the target task, drawn
as a star, and three \SourceCompetitions, drawn as dots. Two smaller
circles represent other domains, each containing three
\SourceCompetitions. Dashed arrows go from the \SourceCompetitionsin the
current domain to a green square labeled domain insight, and from the
\SourceCompetitionsof all domains to a red stack of rectangles labeled
improvement insights; solid arrows go from the square, from the stack,
and from each \SourceCompetitionin the current domain (labeled
competition insights) to the target task.

For a target task, the system receives the domain insight of the task’s
domain, the competition insights of the source competitions in the same
domain, and all improvement insights, which are assembled from the
source competitions of every domain
(Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.2.2. Insight Injection Modes ‣ 4.2. Usage of Insights ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")).
The two injection modes hold the insights, system, prompt, harness,
task, and budget constant, and only change _when_ the competition
insights and improvement insights enter the context; the domain insight
is always in the initial context.

Skill mode. Following the progressive-disclosure design of Agent
Skills ([Anthropic, 2025](#bib.bib19)), the initial context lists only
compact metadata (name and short description) of each available insight.
This mode preserves context for task observations and execution
feedback, but its benefit depends on the system recognizing a relevant
insight from its description and retrieving it.

Playbook mode. Following the use of evolving playbooks as agent
context ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18)), the full texts of all
available insights are rendered directly into the system prompt before
the system begins. This mode removes the retrieval decision and makes
every insight immediately available, at the cost of a longer context
that may contain insights irrelevant to, or inconsistent with, the
target task.

#### 4.2.3. Application to New Competitions

The assembled insights are not tied to MLE-InsightBench: a new
competition from outside it can use them in the same way as a target
task. For one or a few new competitions, the only step needed is to
determine the domain of each competition, either manually or by
embedding its description as in Domain Clustering
(§[3](#S3 "3. MLE-InsightBench: A Controlled-Environment Benchmark ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems"))
and assigning it to the closest cluster; the domain insight and
competition insights of that domain and all improvement insights are
then directly usable without further assembly.

Once a new competition has ended and its writeups and solutions are
available, it can be added as a source competition by an incremental
update that reruns only the affected assembly tasks. MLE-InsightForge
assembles the competition insight of the new competition and
re-synthesizes the domain insight of its domain; if its writeups yield
new raw improvement insights, they are assigned to the existing
clusters, and only the improvement insights of the clusters that receive
them are re-synthesized. Re-clustering is needed only when many
competitions have been added, which may shift the cluster structure, or
when a new competition belongs to no existing domain.

We illustrate the assembly and usage of insights with the competition
Energy Behavior of Prosumers, the target task of the Time Series
Prediction domain. The task asks for hourly forecasts of the electricity
produced and consumed by Estonian customers with solar panels, given
weather forecasts, energy prices, and client data such as the installed
photovoltaic capacity, and is evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE).
Predictions are made through a time-series API that serves the test data
day by day, in which the latest revealed targets and client data lag two
days behind the prediction times. The four source competitions of the
domain forecast COVID-19 cases, microbusiness density, and retail sales,
and none of them involves energy.

Impact on the solutions. Over six runs each, the agentic MLE system
reaches a private-test MAE of 228 $`\pm`$ 76.8 without insights and 64.8

prediction error).
Figure [8(b)](#S4.F8.sf2 "In Figure 8 ‣ 4.3. Running Example ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")
compares the final solutions of a run without insights and a run with
insights, in which all three insights are injected via the playbook

only two hours before each prediction time and joins the client data of
the same day, although the API reveals the targets and client data only
two days later. Its hold-out validation on the training data cannot
detect this mismatch and reports an MAE of 29.24; at prediction time,
the rolling means and the capacity are missing (the client data served
by the API is ignored), filled with zeros, and the private-test MAE
rises to 234.15. The solution with insights makes three changes that
implement the highlighted insight parts:
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
it computes its rolling means only from target lags of at least 48
hours,
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
it learns the production per unit of installed capacity and rescales its
predictions by the capacity, and
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
it joins the client data as of two days earlier, both in training and
from the data served by the API. Its validation MAE (31.91) is worse but
reflects the deployment setting, and its private-test MAE is 57.12.

## 5. Evaluation

We answer the following research questions:

- •
  RQ1: How much do the assembled insights improve the solutions of an
  agentic MLE system?
- •
  RQ2: How do the three types of insights contribute to the improvement?
- •
  RQ3: How do the two injection modes, skills and playbooks, compare in
  effectiveness and cost?
- •
  RQ4: Do the improvements generalize across backend LLMs?

### 5.1. Experimental Setup

Target tasks and system. We evaluate on the 12 held-out target tasks of
MLE-InsightBench
(Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3. MLE-InsightBench: A Controlled-Environment Benchmark ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")),
using the insights that MLE-InsightForge assembled from the 148 source
competitions. The base agentic MLE system is backed by
deepseek-v4-flash-0731. Each run receives one NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (48G
of RAM built with cuda_11.5.r11.5), four AMD EPYC 7343 CPUs (16 cores @
1.5GHz), a 12-hour development budget, and at most 250 agent steps.

|               |          |             |             |
| ------------- | -------- | ----------- | ----------- |
| Mode          | Domain   | Competition | Improvement |
| Baseline      | –        | –           | –           |
| Full-skill    | playbook | skill       | skill       |
| Full-playbook | playbook | playbook    | playbook    |
| D-playbook    | playbook | –           | –           |
| C-playbook    | –        | playbook    | –           |
| I-playbook    | –        | –           | playbook    |

Table 2. Insight injection modes of each condition.

Conditions.
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.1. Experimental Setup ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")
lists the six conditions in our experiments, combining different
injection modes. Baseline receives no insight. Full-skill and
Full-playbook inject all three types of insights, as skills and as a
playbook, respectively
(§[4.2.2](#S4.SS2.SSS2 "4.2.2. Insight Injection Modes ‣ 4.2. Usage of Insights ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")).
Specially, domain insights are always injected as playbook since they
are short and most relevant. The three ablation conditions, D-playbook,
C-playbook, and I-playbook, each inject a single type of insight (domain
insights, competition insights, and improvement insights, respectively)
as a playbook.

Metrics. The primary metric is the private-test score of the final
solution, computed by the task’s MLE-bench-compatible grader. Because
raw scores are not comparable across MLE-InsightBench tasks, we min–max
normalize the scores of each task on a fixed range, after reversing
lower-is-better metrics, and compute the average improvement over the
baseline for each mode across all tasks:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (1) |     |

````math
\Delta=\frac{\Delta_{m}-\Delta_{Baseline}}{\Delta_{Baseline}}\times 100\%,\quad\Delta_{m}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}N_{m,t,k},\quad N_{m,t,k}=\frac{x_{m,t,k}-L_{t}}{U_{t}-L_{t}},
``` |  |

where $`\Delta_{m}`$ and $`\Delta_{Baseline}`$ denote the average
normalized scores of mode $`m`$ and Baseline over $`T`$ tasks ($`T=12`$)
and $`K`$ repetitions ($`K=6`$), $`N_{m,t,k}`$ and $`x_{m,t,k}`$ are the
normalized and raw scores of mode $`m`$ on task $`t`$ in the $`k`$-th
run, and $`L_{t}`$ and $`U_{t}`$ are the worst and best scores over the
runs of Baseline, Full-skill, and Full-playbook on task $`t`$. The same
range is used for every condition to put all conditions on one scale, so
an ablation run outside it may be normalized to below 0 or above 1.

To measure cost, we record the input, reasoning, and output tokens
consumed by the backend LLM and the wall-clock time of each run. We
convert the tokens to a monetary cost at the OpenRouter API prices of
deepseek-v4-flash-0731: \$0.44 per million uncached input tokens,
\$0.014 per million cached input tokens, and \$1.32 per million output
tokens, where the output tokens include the reasoning tokens. For each
task and condition, we report the mean with a 95% Student-$`t`$
confidence interval, and compare each condition with Baseline using a
two-sided Mann–Whitney $`U`$ test ([Mann and Whitney, 1947](#bib.bib56))
at $`\alpha=0.05`$. Since each condition is compared with Baseline on 12
tasks, we also report the number of significant tasks after the
Holm–Bonferroni correction ([Holm, 1979](#bib.bib40)) over the tasks of
each condition. Every condition has 72 runs, i.e., six runs per task. In
addition to the private-test score of the final solution, we analyze the
validation scores that the system measures on its own validation split
for every scored candidate solution during development, which show how
the solution quality evolves over time. The validation scores are
normalized in the same way as private-test scores; at each minute, we
take the median over the runs of a task and average it over tasks.

Tables [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.1. Experimental Setup ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")

0.302 for Baseline to 0.676 for Full-skill (123.9%) and 0.673 for

Full-skill improves the mean score on 12 of the 12 tasks, significantly

Series S01E01 as the only task where the improvement is not significant;
Full-playbook improves on 11 tasks, significantly on 11 (10 after the
correction). The largest gains occur on tasks, such as Image Matching
2025 and Energy Behavior of Prosumers, where the validation design and
task-specific modeling choices documented in peer competitions are
consequential.

b) shows that the insights help both in drafting the initial solution
and in improving it: the first scored solutions of Full-skill and
Full-playbook are 1.8 and 2.9 points above those of Baseline; they reach
the final best score of Baseline after 80 and 40 minutes, and end with
gains of 7.8 and 5.9 points over the first solution of Baseline,
compared with 3.3 points for Baseline itself.

### 5.4. RQ3: Comparison of Injection Modes

Overall, the two injection modes reach similar normalized scores (0.676
for Full-skill and 0.673 for Full-playbook in
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.1. Experimental Setup ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")),
but the better mode varies across tasks. Full-playbook has the higher
mean score on 6 tasks and Full-skill on 6; notably, Full-playbook falls
below Baseline on POG Series S01E01 (though not significantly), whereas
Full-skill stays above it. A playbook guarantees that every insight is
seen but can steer the system toward insights that do not fit the task,
whereas skills let the system skip irrelevant insights but depend on it
retrieving the relevant ones. Although Full-skill reaches a similar
score to Full-playbook, its trajectories show that the system rarely
retrieves the full text of a skill: only 19 of its 72 runs call
read_skill at all, 14 of them to read a competition insight (typically
that of the most similar source competition, e.g., Image Matching
Challenge 2024 ([Bellavia et al., 2024](#bib.bib58)) for Image Matching
2025) and 5 to read an improvement insight. The improvement of
Full-skill therefore stems mostly from what every run receives in its
initial context rather than from the retrieved texts: the domain
insight, with which D-playbook alone reaches 0.595, and the metadata of
the skills, whose descriptions state when each insight applies, e.g.,
the problem that each improvement insight resolves. The two modes also
lead to different correct predictions
(Figure [10](#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 5.3. RQ2: Contribution of Insight Types ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")(a)):
5,376 private-test items are predicted correctly only by Full-skill and
4,918 only by Full-playbook, compared with 3,838 only by Baseline.

The two modes differ in cost. Relative to Baseline, Full-skill increases
the per-task input tokens by only 7.7%, whereas Full-playbook increases
them by 25.2%, because the playbook is carried in the context of every
model call; the output tokens and time are similar
(Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.1. Experimental Setup ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")).
The per-task cost is only \$1.72, \$1.88, and \$1.95, respectively, as
most input tokens hit the prompt cache.

As shown in
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.5. RQ4: Generalizability across LLMs ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems"),
the insights are not specific to one backend LLM: on the normalized
scale over both tasks, they also improve GPT-6.1-Sol by 80.3% with
Full-skill and 61.9% with Full-playbook. GPT-6.1-Sol is a stronger
backend than deepseek-v4-flash-0731 on Image Matching 2025: its Baseline
already reaches an mAA of 42.8, close to the gold-medal threshold of the
human leaderboard (43.34). Although the improvement is smaller than with
deepseek-v4-flash-0731, the insights still significantly improve the
normalized score by 427.9% with Full-skill and 326.9% with
Full-playbook, lifting the mean mAA beyond the gold-medal threshold
(52.0 and 49.9). On POG Series S01E01, where the insights do not help
deepseek-v4-flash-0731, they improve the normalized score of GPT-6.1-Sol
by 38.2% with Full-skill and 29.8% with Full-playbook, although not
significantly over six runs; this suggests that a stronger backend LLM
can make better use of the insights. Still, no condition with either
backend LLM reaches the median of the human leaderboard on this task
(MAE 0.016845), so the tasks of MLE-InsightBench remain challenging for
future agentic MLE systems. Unlike deepseek-v4-flash-0731, GPT-6.1-Sol
actively retrieves skills: 12 of its 12 Full-skill runs call read_skill
(12 for improvement insights and 6 for competition insights), which may
explain why Full-skill beats Full-playbook with GPT-6.1-Sol on both
tasks.

The two backend LLMs also develop solutions differently: on Image
Matching 2025, GPT-6.1-Sol creates its first solution node earlier
(median step 19 vs. 165), uses most of the 12-hour budget (594–629
minutes), and tries 9.2–13.3 solution nodes per run, whereas
deepseek-v4-flash-0731 usually submits its final solution after 210–320
minutes with 2.5–4.0 nodes.

## 6. Limitations

Task scope. MLE-InsightBench is derived from Kaggle competitions, which
provide realistic end-to-end MLE tasks but do not represent every
production setting. Kaggle emphasizes predictive performance under a
fixed metric and submission interface, whereas deployed machine learning
systems also require maintainability, monitoring, fairness, and privacy.

Domain construction. The domains of MLE-InsightBench are induced by
clustering competition descriptions. Other representations or clustering
choices could change which competitions are considered closely related
and thus contribute insights to a target task.

Insight quality. The insights are assembled by an LLM-based agent. To
reduce the risk of hallucination and misrepresentation, MLE-InsightForge
must read every required source in full and back each insight with an
evidence record, which links the insight to the human-written passages
it is based on and makes it traceable.

Leakage beyond the benchmark. MLE-InsightBench excludes the materials of
every target task from the insight sources, but it cannot control what
the backend LLMs have learned during pre-training. Because Kaggle
writeups and notebooks are public, a backend LLM may have seen solutions
of the target tasks; this affects all conditions equally, including
Baseline, and therefore may inflate absolute scores. Selecting the most
recent eligible competition of each domain as the target task reduces,
but does not eliminate, this risk.

Models and costs. The main results use one backend LLM for the agentic
MLE system and one LLM for MLE-InsightForge, so they may depend on these
models’ knowledge, tool-use behavior, and long-context capabilities; RQ4
studies the former dependency. The 12-hour, GPU-backed budget also
limits accessibility and may favor approaches that spend more compute.
Assembling the insights from all 148 source competitions with
gpt-5.6-sol-pro cost \$903 USD (\$1,544 USD including runs repeated
during development), a one-time cost that is amortized over all tasks of
a domain. The experiments are also costly: with deepseek-v4-flash-0731,
each condition takes 11.4–16.9 GPU days and \$124–\$144 in API costs,
and with GPT-6.1-Sol, the API costs of a condition on all 12 target
tasks would reach \$957, extrapolated from up to \$160 on two tasks.
Running MLE-InsightForge with a different backend LLM may yield
different findings, which our budget precludes evaluating; to facilitate
reproduction and such evaluations by others, we open-source our workflow
and insights.

## 7. Related Work

Agentic MLE. MLAgentBench ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)) evaluates
LLM agents that design, run, and revise ML experiments, and
MLE-bench ([Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)) evaluates end-to-end
solutions of Kaggle competitions against private-test labels. The
systems on the MLE-bench leaderboard mostly advance the search over
candidate solutions ([Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib8); [Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20); [Toledo et al., 2025](#bib.bib28); [Li et al.,
2025](#bib.bib14); [Wan et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27)) and, increasingly, the use of insights from other
tasks
(§[2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2. Insights in Agentic MLE Systems ‣ 2. Background ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems")).
Systems that use insights couple a particular source of insights with a
particular agent scaffold, and evaluate the combination as a whole on
MLE-bench. Our work is complementary: rather than proposing another
scaffold, we hold the agentic MLE system fixed and study how the
assembled insights, their types, and their injection modes affect it on
a benchmark whose source competitions are fixed and disjoint from the
target tasks.

Program synthesis for ML code. Before LLM agents, program synthesis
targeted ML code by searching a restricted space of programs.
BLAZE ([Wang et al., 2018](#bib.bib59)) synthesizes tensor
transformations in a MATLAB-like DSL from input–output examples, and
TF-Coder ([Shi et al., 2022](#bib.bib60)) enumerates expressions over
TensorFlow operations, prioritized by learned models; INTENT ([Zhou et
al., 2022](#bib.bib62)) lets users decompose hard tensor
transformations, and HySynth ([Barke et al., 2024](#bib.bib63)) guides
the search with a grammar learned from LLM completions. Nam et al. ([Nam
et al., 2022](#bib.bib61)) predict the sequence of PyTorch and
TensorFlow API calls that transforms the inputs into the outputs to
guide enumerative search. At a coarser granularity, AutoML-Zero ([Real
et al., 2020](#bib.bib64)) evolves complete ML algorithms from basic
mathematical operations, NEAR ([Shah et al., 2020](#bib.bib65)) and
dPADS ([Cui and Zhu, 2021](#bib.bib66)) search for differentiable
programs in a DSL, and Marinescu et al. ([Marinescu et al.,
2021](#bib.bib67)) search ML pipelines defined by a context-free
grammar. These techniques synthesize short programs or pipelines within
a predefined search space, whereas an agentic MLE system writes an
end-to-end solution in a general-purpose language; the insights
assembled by MLE-InsightForge play a role similar to their learned
priors, steering the system toward decisions that worked on related
tasks.

Experience, memory, and context for LLM agents. Reflexion ([Shinn et
al., 2023](#bib.bib6)) stores verbal feedback from earlier trials of the
same task, ExpeL ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)) extracts
natural-language lessons from successful and failed trajectories and
retrieves them for new tasks, and Agent Workflow Memory ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3)) induces reusable workflows from past trajectories.
ACE ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18)) treats the agent’s context as an
evolving playbook that is incrementally refined from execution feedback,
and Agent Skills ([Anthropic, 2025](#bib.bib19)) package instructions
and resources that the agent loads on demand. These approaches mainly
learn from the agent’s own trajectories. MLE-InsightForge instead
assembles insights from human-written solutions and writeups of peer
tasks, organizes them into domain, competition, and improvement
insights, and compares the skill and playbook modes of injecting the
same insights.

Mining Kaggle artifacts. DistilKaggle ([Mostafavi Ghahfarokhi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib9)) curates Kaggle notebooks together with code-quality
measures, and Jin et al. ([Jin et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)) mine Kaggle
notebooks and use MLE-bench-style grading to study their reproducibility
under modern execution environments. We use Kaggle descriptions,
writeups, and top solutions as sources from which to assemble insights
for solving unseen tasks.

Data contamination in benchmarks. Contamination of evaluation data
threatens the validity of LLM benchmarks, and LiveCodeBench ([Jain et
al., 2025](#bib.bib39)) mitigates it by continuously collecting problems
released after the models’ training cutoffs. For agentic MLE systems,
the relevant contamination also comes from insight sources available at
solving time
(§[2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3. Data Leakage in Evaluating Agentic MLE Systems ‣ 2. Background ‣ Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems"));
MLE-InsightBench controls these sources by construction, using only
causal non-descendants of the target tasks as sources.

## 8. Conclusion

We studied how insights assembled from closely-related MLE tasks affect
an agentic MLE system. We collected MLE-InsightBench, whose held-out
split of 160 Kaggle competitions in 12 domains keeps target task
information out of the insights, and designed MLE-InsightForge, an agent
that assembles evidence-backed domain insights, competition insights,
and improvement insights from the source competitions and injects them
as skills or a playbook. The assembled insights improve the normalized
private-test score by 123.9% as skills and 122.8% as a playbook; the
three types of insights are complementary, skills are more
cost-effective, and the improvements generalize. These findings suggest
treating insight assembly as an explicit component of agentic MLE
systems whose sources are controlled in evaluations.
````
